shape.name: Shape E — Receptive Skills (Reading)
shape.description: Traditional receptive skills lesson focusing on practicing reading sub-skills.
shape.pedagogical_justification: This lesson practices reading sub-skills (predicting content, identifying instruction words in questions, reading for detail) using a B1-level news article about Thailand's falling birth rate. Students pre-teach key vocabulary, apply prediction and keyword-underlining strategies, then read and answer 8 multiple-choice comprehension questions. The article provides authentic input on a relevant social issue, and the post-reading discussion stage encourages students to connect the content to their own views. The lesson follows the traditional receptive skills structure: lead-in → pre-reading (vocab + strategies) → while-reading → post-reading (answers + discussion).
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practiced and developed the sub-skills of reading for detail and specific information in the context of an article about Thailand's falling birth rate.

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will have practiced and developed the sub-skills of reading for detail and specific information in the context of an article about Thailand's falling birth rate.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
24 July, 2026
Duration:
45 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
E (Receptive Skills — Reading)
Materials:
Reading test paper (Why People Stopped Having Kids), slideshow (reveal.js), audio recording of article (male US voice), timer plugin
Assessment:
Reading comprehension CA (8 multiple-choice questions)
Skills:
Reading

stages.stage_aim: To activate schemata about family size in Thailand and introduce the topic
procedure: Show splash slide: image of mother holding child (silhouette at sunset). Ask: What do you see? What might this lesson be about?
Advance to title slide: 'Thailand is having a problem with its birth rate.' Confirm the topic.
Show importance slide: why this topic matters (social issue, difficult exam questions).
Pair discussion: In your experience, how many children do Thai families usually have? Is this changing? Why? 2 min. Elicit a few ideas.

stages.stage_aim: To pre-teach four key vocabulary items from the text
procedure: Transition slide: 'Let's check your word knowledge' (red background).
Present 4 key words using 3-click reveal: phonemic script → word in box → context sentence.
Words: fertility (/fɜːˈtɪləti/), crisis (/ˈkraɪsɪs/), isolated (/ˈaɪsəleɪtɪd/), pension (/ˈpenʃən/).
For each word: show phonemic script first, click to reveal English word, click again for context sentence with clarifying second clause.
Ask CCQs for each word: High fertility = many babies or few? Is a crisis a big problem or small problem? etc.

stages.stage_aim: To teach and practice predicting content and identifying instruction words in questions
procedure: Strategy 1 — Predict: Do/Why/How table. 'Predict the main idea before you read. It prepares your brain. Read the title and look at the picture.'
Auto-animate demo: Show 4 predictions based on the title. Students predict which make sense. Click to reveal checkmarks on plausible options.
Strategy 2 — Underline key words: Do/Why/How table. 'Underline instruction words. They tell you what type of answer to look for.'
Auto-animate demo: 3 example questions with key words (main purpose, probably true, mean) in plain spans. Click to reveal underlined key words.
Explain: purpose = look for overall aim. probably = inference, not directly stated. mean = vocabulary in context.

stages.stage_aim: To read for detail and answer multiple-choice comprehension questions
procedure: Transition slide: 'Read the article.' (red background). Hand out test paper.
Students can listen to the audio recording (male US voice reading the article) using the audio player on the slide, or read silently.
Students read the article and answer 8 multiple-choice questions.
Timer: 10 minutes (auto-starts). Teacher walks around and monitors.
After 10 min, transition to answer checking.

stages.stage_aim: To check comprehension answers with explanations and text evidence
procedure: Transition: 'Check your answers.' (red background). Students swap worksheets.
Go through each question one by one (green background slides).
Each answer slide shows: Question text → Correct answer (letter + full sentence) → Explanation (why this answer is correct, with text evidence) → Text excerpt.
Q1: D — 0.8 children (fewer than one). Key: 'one of the lowest' not 'the lowest.'
Q2: A — Choice, not war/disease/famine. Key: 'This time, it is happening by choice. That is new.'
Q3: C — Main purpose = explain causes and consequences. Article structure: situation → causes → effects.
Q4: D — Economic (growth, pensions) + human (loneliness). Key: 'But the human cost may be even worse.'
Q5: C — Social isolation = being separated from others. Key: 'less time with others.'
Q6: B — Fewer marriages lead to fewer births. Key: 'most people still have children after marriage.'
Q7: A — Payments help but aren't enough. Key: 'but no government policy has replaced what community provides.'
Q8: B — Thailand's falling birth rate. Key: 'What Thailand is facing is a warning.'
Collect scores.

stages.stage_aim: To discuss personal opinions about the article's topic
procedure: Transition: purple background slide with discussion prompts.
In pairs, students discuss: Why do fewer people in Thailand want to have children? What could the government do?
Timer: 7 minutes.
Teacher walks around and monitors, notes good language and errors.
Elicit a few opinions from different pairs. Content + language feedback.

materials: Reading test paper: Why People Stopped Having Kids (adapted from The Washington Post)
Audio recording of reading passage (Alex, US male voice)
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practiced and developed the sub-skills of reading for detail and specific information in the context of an article about Thailand's falling birth rate.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: To develop prediction and keyword-identification strategies for reading comprehension questions.
answer_key: Q1: D — They have fewer than one child on average. The first paragraph states the average is 0.8 children — less than one. Option A says 'the lowest' but the text says 'one of the lowest.'
Q2: A — People are choosing to have fewer children on purpose. Paragraph 3 explains past drops were due to war, disease, or famine, but 'this time, it is happening by choice. That is new.'
Q3: C — To explain the causes and consequences of falling birth rates. The article follows a classic explainer structure: situation (paras 1-2), causes (paras 5-6), consequences (para 4).
Q4: D — Falling birth rates affect both the economy and people's happiness. Paragraph 4 gives economic effects (slower growth, pensions) and human effects (loneliness, isolation).
Q5: C — Being separated from other people in daily life. The paragraph explains that phones keep people in their rooms, leading to 'less time with others.'
Q6: B — Fewer marriages are likely to lead to fewer births. The text says 'most people still have children after marriage,' so fewer marriages means fewer children.
Q7: A — Paying parents is not the full answer by itself. The author says payments encourage births 'but no government policy has replaced what community provides.'
Q8: B — Thailand's falling birth rate. Fernández-Villaverde says Thailand's situation is 'the only thing that matters.' The whole article is about the birth rate crisis.
